analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share the diagnostic and repair information needed to fix your own car.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote despite 53 bipartisan cosponsors, and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: As cars became computerized, manufacturers kept diagnostic codes and repair information locked up, so independent mechanics and car owners often had no choice but to use dealer service departments. The bill would have required manufacturers to disclose the information needed to diagnose, service, and repair a vehicle to owners and repair shops, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules and enforcing violations. It included trade-secret protections and a private right of action for repair shops and vehicle owners. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners, who could shop among competing repair shops instead of being steered to dealers, and independent repair shops and the aftermarket parts industry, which the bill's own findings say employ over 5 million workers in 495,000 businesses and generate $200 billion in annual sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must promptly disclose to owners, repair facilities, and the FTC all information necessary to diagnose, service, or repair a vehicle, including codes needed to integrate replacement equipment [S2] [S3].
The FTC must write uniform disclosure rules within 180 days, covering written and internet disclosure, applying to vehicles from model year 1994 onward [S3].

Noncompliance is defined as an unfair method of competition and an unfair or deceptive act under the FTC Act, and owners or repair shops can sue in federal court to stop violations and recover attorney fees, no matter how small the amount in dispute [S2] [S3].
The bill's findings state that access codes increasingly prevent owners from getting timely, affordable repairs, and that restricting repair information limits consumer choice and competition [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of disclosing repair information and lose the leverage that pushes repair business to their franchised dealers, and dealer service departments that would face more competition.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would bear real compliance costs to document and publish repair information, and the bill preserves trade secrets only at the FTC's discretion, which automakers argued risked exposing proprietary designs [S2] [S3].
A private right of action with attorney fees for any repair facility, regardless of the amount in controversy, invites litigation that manufacturers would likely contest aggressively [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For car owners, the benefit is straightforward: repair competition and the freedom to fix a car anywhere, at a lower price. The costs fall mostly on manufacturers and dealers, though honest supporters would acknowledge the compliance burden and litigation exposure are real. The bill's carve-out for EPA emissions diagnostics rules showed an attempt to avoid conflicting with existing regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 2, 2001, by Rep. Joe Barton with bipartisan original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
On August 10, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it stayed [S5].
It drew 53 cosponsors, split almost evenly between 24 Democrats and 29 Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died without a committee or floor vote [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their franchised dealers are better off, because they kept control of repair and diagnostic information and faced no disclosure mandate. Car owners and independent shops gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and subcommittee without action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Automakers and their dealer networks
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair legislation and backed the competing voluntary disclosure approach

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the bill was sponsored by a Republican with Democratic cosponsors, and its 53 cosponsors split 29 Republican and 24 Democratic.

industries.note: They would have to hand over diagnostic and repair information they currently control, ending the ability to steer repairs to franchised dealers through locked access codes.
They profit from being among the few shops able to service computerized systems; mandated disclosure would open that work to competition.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and the auto parts aftermarket
industries.note: The bill gives them the information needed to repair modern vehicles, and the bill's findings credit the aftermarket with 5 million jobs and $200 billion in annual sales.
